nameStory: The Red-necked Stint gets its name from the rusty-red or rufous coloring that appears on its neck and head during breeding season. The word 'stint' comes from an old English term for small sandpipers, possibly related to 'stunt,' referring to their compact size compared to other shorebirds.
description: The Red-necked Stint is one of the world's smallest sandpipers, about the size of a sparrow. This tiny shorebird has a straight, thin black bill and dark legs, with brownish upperparts and white underparts. During breeding season, it develops a distinctive rusty-red wash on its neck and head. As an extreme rarity in New England with only 11 recorded observations, spotting one would be a once-in-a-lifetime birding experience.

idTips.label: Breeding plumage neck
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, shows a warm rusty-red or orange-red wash across the neck, throat, and sides of head that feels almost glowing in good light

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than most other sandpipers, appearing almost delicate and sparrow-sized when mixed with other shorebirds

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Short, straight, needle-thin black bill that looks proportionally small even for this tiny bird

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Dark blackish legs that appear thin and wire-like, contrasting with the pale underparts

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Shows thin white wing stripes in flight and appears to flutter more rapidly than larger sandpipers due to its small size

habitat: In New England, Red-necked Stints would most likely appear on mudflats, sandy beaches, or shallow pools during migration. They prefer areas with soft substrate where they can probe for small invertebrates, often mixing with flocks of other small sandpipers along the coast.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant during spring migration (May-June), when birds would show developing or full rusty-red neck coloring. Any sighting would be exceptional.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during summer, as breeding occurs in arctic Russia. Any summer record would be extraordinary.
seasonality.fall: Most likely season for vagrant appearances (August-September), though still extremely rare. Birds would be in duller, brownish plumage without the red neck.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England winters, as the species winters in Southeast Asia and Australia. Any winter sighting would be unprecedented.

funFact: Red-necked Stints make one of the longest migrations of any bird relative to their body size, with some individuals flying over 6,000 miles from Alaska to Australia - that's like a hummingbird flying to the moon in terms of body-length-to-distance ratio!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Least Sandpiper, but Red-necked Stint has dark legs (not yellowish) and a more rufous neck in breeding plumage. Remember: 'Red-necked has dark legs, Least has light legs' - opposite of what you might expect from their names!
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily an Asian species that very rarely strays to North America, making any New England sighting a major birding event. Most North American records occur on the West Coast, so an East Coast appearance would be especially noteworthy and should be carefully documented and reported to birding authorities.
compareHints: Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper. Its breeding plumage is more intensely rufous on the neck than Western Sandpiper, and it lacks the streaky breast pattern of Baird's Sandpiper. The combination of tiny size, dark legs, and rusty neck (in breeding plumage) helps separate it from all regular New England species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
